title: Most of the meaning survives compression
summary: What 404,290 Quora question pairs taught me about trading accuracy for speed.

body: My Master’s project started with a simple question: do you really need a heavy model to spot duplicate questions? The strongest published detectors use deep networks. They are accurate, and they are expensive to train and to serve.

I worked with the Quora Question Pairs dataset: 404,290 pairs, about 37% of them duplicates. Each question became FastText word vectors, each pair became 1,200 features, and then Principal Component Analysis squeezed those features down before a classifier made the call.

items.title: The baseline
items.detail: XGBoost on all 1,200 features reached 84.01% accuracy.

items.title: The compressed version
items.detail: At 200 dimensions it reached 83.68%, a third of a percentage point lower.

items.title: The cost
items.detail: Training time fell by 66.7% on average and memory by 83.4%, from 3.2 GB to 0.53 GB.

body: The number I keep coming back to is not the accuracy. It is the shape of the trade-off: throw away five sixths of the features and you lose almost nothing. Most of the meaning survives.
It changed how I evaluate models at work too. A model that is slightly better but too expensive to run has not really solved the problem. Cost belongs in the evaluation from day one.
